title: Parallel transcoding of one stream across workers
description: When a job runs below about 1.2x real time, helper jobs on other workers encode later chunks of the same film, so CPU on every node serves one viewer. Deterministic segments let the chunks splice.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building (chunk boundaries, slots, cancellation, read-ahead, failover of a helper)
Three worker processes encode one film in chunks; the assembled segments equal a single worker's video byte for byte
hls.js plays through and seeks across chunk boundaries with no stall or discontinuity
A helper killed mid-chunk is replaced and the viewer keeps playing
Helpers never take the last free slot from a new viewer
Measured speedup with 1, 2 and 3 workers in the PR
notes: The user's idea: use CPU on all nodes rather than relying on a GPU. 'Gotta test sharding streams.' Built 2026-11-08: a job below 1.2x real time (judged after 2 s of output) inserts a helper row for the next free 4-segment chunk within the viewer's lead; helpers are claimed by other workers first and never take a worker's last free slot. A job's ffmpeg runs on across chunk starts until it reaches a chunk another job holds, so a job nobody helps is one ffmpeg. Measured with each worker's ffmpeg pinned to one CPU: 1 worker 16.3 s, 2 workers 10.4 s (1.57x), 3 workers 8.0 s (2.03x). Re-encoded segments from different runs have the same frames and frame times within 1 ms, not the same bytes (x264 stays multi-threaded). A burnt image subtitle gets no helpers (a run that starts mid-film loses the cue showing at its start); JS-071 closes that gap. A failed helper does not fail the viewer's spec and blocks re-helping its chunk for 30 s. Backlog: helpers are a fixed threshold (1.2x), not a measure of spare capacity across the cluster; a helper's chunk that the viewer never reaches is wasted work until the idle kill; per-helper metrics (JS-021 traces should show which chunks were helped and why).
